title: Congruence by Rigid Motions
short: Two figures are congruent if a sequence of rigid motions maps one onto the other.

blocks.html: Translations, reflections and rotations are called rigid motions. They give a precise meaning to “same size and same shape.”

A rigid motion moves a figure without stretching or bending it, so it never changes a length or an angle. If a sequence of rigid motions carries one figure exactly onto another, then every side and every angle of one matches a side and an angle of the other. That is what we mean by congruent.

Two figures are congruent if a sequence of rigid motions maps one onto the other. Corresponding sides and angles are equal. In $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$, the letters match in order: $A$ with $D$, $B$ with $E$, $C$ with $F$.

blocks.name: transform
blocks.cap: Pick a motion that puts the triangle exactly on the dashed outline.

blocks.title: Two moves in a row
blocks.q: Reflect $(2, 3)$ across the $y$-axis, then translate the image 4 units down.

blocks.title: Show two triangles are congruent
blocks.q: $\triangle ABC$ has $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$, $C(1, 3)$; $\triangle DEF$ has $D(-1, -1)$, $E(-4, -1)$, $F(-1, -3)$. Are they congruent?
steps: Try a $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin, $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$.
It sends $A \to D$, $B \to E$ and $C \to F$.
A rigid motion maps one onto the other.

blocks.title: Use the matching parts
blocks.q: $\triangle PQR \cong \triangle XYZ$, with $PQ = 7$ and $\angle R = 40^\circ$. Find $XY$ and $\angle Z$.

blocks.html: Assuming the order of moves doesn’t matter. Reflecting across the $y$-axis and then translating 3 right sends $(1, 0)$ to $(2, 0)$, but translating first and then reflecting sends it to $(-4, 0)$. Do the moves in the order given.
